title: Fine Motor & Threading
strapline: Little fingers doing big work — every bead threaded is a step towards buttons, scissors and writing.
intent: Children strengthen the small muscles of hands and fingers that later hold a pencil, fasten a coat and cut along a line.
Children refine hand-eye coordination and the pincer grip through threading, posting, pinching and twisting.
Children learn to use one-handed tools — scissors, tweezers, hole punches, droppers — with control and intent.
Children build patience and persistence: threading is fiddly, and finishing anyway is the point.
Children slip into early maths through their hands — bead patterns, counting on the lace, comparing whose string is longer.
implementation: Graduate the challenge: chunky beads on rigid dowels, then laces with taped ends, then small beads, buttons and pasta on fine string.
Sit alongside and narrate the technique quietly — 'pinch the lace, poke it through, pull it out the other side' — then hush and let hands work.
Stiffen lace ends with tape and hold the first bead as an anchor so early efforts don't slide straight off — nothing kills persistence like losing your beads.
Offer scissor work daily at the same table: snipping playdough sausages and grass before paper, then along drawn lines.
Watch grips without rushing them — fist to fingers comes with strength, so build the strength (tweezers, pegs, dough) rather than correcting the hold.
Start a simple bead pattern — red, blue, red, blue — and wonder aloud what comes next.
Celebrate the finished string properly: wear it, photograph it, hang it up — the product matters to the child even when the process was the point.
key_questions: Which bead will you choose next?
How did you get the lace through such a tiny hole?
Whose string is longer — how could we check?
What pattern is your necklace making?
That bit was tricky — what did you do to make it work?

impact.text: Younger children thread large beads, pour and use one-handed tools with growing control.
Children snip with scissors, their grip moving from whole fist towards fingers.
Older children cut along a drawn line and hold mark-making tools with a comfortable, effective grip.
Children choose the right tool for the job — tweezers for the tiny pompoms, the hole punch for their ticket — and use it with intent.
Children thread small beads and manage fiddly fastenings with precision and patience.
Children copy and create repeating patterns along their string and say what comes next.
Children count beads as they thread and compare whose string is longer.
Children stay with a tricky thread until it's done and announce 'I did it!' with real pride.

enhancements: A threading tree — a branch in a pot for hanging finished bead strings, growing fuller through the week.
Nature threading: leaves, drilled conkers and hooped seed pods on garden string.
A jewellery shop role-play add-on — price tags, a till and a mirror, so necklaces need making, pricing and selling.
Tweezer transfer games: pompoms into ice-cube trays, one per hole.
Big-stitch sewing cards of the children's own laminated drawings, holes punched around the edge.
Nuts, bolts and jam-jar lids for twisting — the rotation that later manages taps and toothpaste.
A crocodile line of pegs at child height for hanging the dolls' washing.

playing_exploring: Beautiful beads and real tools pull children in — the strengthening happens because they can't resist the materials.
Children test their own limits: smaller beads, longer strings, tinier tweezers.
active_learning: Threading rewards persistence bead by bead — every success is visible on the string.
Children set their own goal ('a necklace for mummy') and see it through.
creating_thinking: Children plan patterns and designs before they thread, holding an idea in mind.
They find their own fixes when the lace frays or the bead jams — twist it, lick it, turn it round.
